newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei stages another dive, falls 1.14 pct.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei stages another dive, falls 1.14 pct.

text.p: Tokyo stocks staged another dive on Wednesday, with the key stock index closing 1.14 percent lower.
Brokers said growing worries over construction firms and financial institutions, already suffering from bad loan problems, overshadowed the market, brokers said.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 average shed 215.81 points or 1.14 percent to close at 18,680.38, its lowest close since November 29, 1995, when the index ended at 18,533.98.
It briefly slipped to 18,555.80 on Wednesday. Its March futures lost 160 points to end at 18,720.
"Unless shares in the (financial and building) sectors stop sliding, overall sentiment will not recover," said Michio Sugita, head of stock trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Brokers said the current market woes, sparked late last year by worries over the country's possible economic slowdown in the first half of 1997, accelerated sales from investors already worried about government policies to boost the economy.
Some also said that public funds were currently the only buyers in the market.
Turnover was about 386 million shares on Wednesday on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange, up from 288 million shares on Tuesday.
Losing sectors overwhelmed gainers 950 to 207, while 96 issues were unchanged.
In other indices, the TOPIX index of all first section stocks dropped 19.77 points or 1.36 percent to 1,433.28. The Nikkei 300 average lost 3.61 points or 1.31 percent to 272.99.
The market's fall has fueled worries that it could delay write-offs of heavy bad debts held by banks and construction firms, as the drop has reduced the value of their share holdings, brokers said.
They also said they were discouraged by a comment from a Finance Ministry official that the recent decline in Tokyo share prices was unlikely to spark worries about Japan's financial system.
"I don't think (the recent stock declines) will lead to worries about the nation's financial system as a whole," the official told Reuters.
Brokers said the comment suggested that the financial authorities did not think it urgent to tackle the spreading worries over the economy.

They also said the focus would now be Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's speech at the start of a new parliamentary session on January 20. "The current downturn was triggered by the market's distrust in the government's policies," said Kenichi Sagami, general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.

The market will wait and see if the government suggests any fiscal or administrative measures to support the economy, such as launching a supplementary budget or further revamping the taxation system, Sagami said.
Later on Wednesday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference that the government will keep careful watch over stock prices.
As for sectors, decliners were led by sea transport, construction, securities, ship building and rubber. The banking sector was the 10th largest losing sector.
The only major gaining sector was credit/lease.
Some global blue-chip issues stood out amid the overall gloom in the market.

Shares in Sony Corp gained 50 yen to close at 7,690 yen, while Nikon Corp shares rose 40 yen to end at 1,530 yen. Advantest Corp soared 300 yen to 5,930 yen by the end of the session, ranking as the third percentage gainer on the first section.
The second section index fell 23.84 points, ending at 1,802.43 with 7.58 million shares traded. The over-the-counter (OTC) index fell 12.05 points to 1,315.11.
-- Hiroko Nakata, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-8027
